Dmitri's mother, Vera, 82, is in the ICU with end-stage heart and kidney failure. After a cardiac arrest three days ago she is on a ventilator and daily dialysis, drifting in and out and no longer able to speak for herself. She left no advance directive, and what she said over the years pulls both ways: after her own sister's long, machine-bound hospital death she told Dmitri, "Don't ever let them keep me going like that"; but only a year ago, shaken after a health scare, she gripped his hand and said, "Promise me you won't give up on me — you fight for me." The intensivist and nephrologist independently agree there is no path to recovery: the machines are prolonging her dying, not reversing it. Dmitri's aunt is adamant: "If you stop the dialysis you are killing your own mother — you'll starve her body of what it needs." The ICU team asks Dmitri for a direction by tomorrow's rounds; comfort-focused care is available whenever he chooses it. Dmitri asks you: "She told me two different things, and now she can't tell me which she meant. How do I decide — by tomorrow — what she would truly want, and whether letting the machines stop is faithfulness or failure?"

reference_answers.label: Reference answer — withdraw-to-comfort (Rae proportionality + Grudem letting-die)
reference_answers.text: Dmitri, begin with the two things she told you, because they are less a contradiction than two versions of one fear. "Don't keep me going like that" named a dread of exactly this machine-bound dying; "don't give up on me" asked you not to abandon her or stop loving her toward life. Withdrawing support when there is no recovery does not abandon her — it refuses to let a machine, rather than your love, be the last thing that holds her. So weigh which fear this moment actually answers, and confirm the facts before you act: she is not in a scare she might come back from; ask the two specialists directly whether another day could change anything and whether any reversible factor has been missed. If the answer holds — and independently given, it likely will — that settles what the machines now *are*. When an intervention can only prolong an irreversible dying and imposes real burden, there is no obligation to continue it; earthly life is a genuine but penultimate good, not one to be preserved at every cost. Withdrawing is not killing her: she will die of the heart and kidney failure already ending her life, and removing what only prolongs that is letting die — distinct in intent and cause from actively killing. So a faithful decision is comfort-focused care: stop the dialysis and, with the team's guidance, the ventilator, and give everything to her peace, presence, and freedom from pain. Two things keep this honest. First, your aunt is not wicked for hearing "withdrawal" as "abandonment" — walk her gently through the killing/letting-die distinction, and do not win the argument and lose your aunt. Second, name the remainder rather than bury it: this is still your mother, and letting her go is a grief, not a technicality — it costs you the hope you have been holding, and that loss is real and worth grieving before God and with your family.

reference_answers.text:
Dmitri, you may well arrive at withdrawal — that is a legitimate Christian option here — but you do not have to reach it by tomorrow's rounds, and it can be right to say so. Two facts counsel a short, deliberate pause rather than an immediate stop: your mother's own words pull in two directions — "don't keep me going like that" and "don't give up on me" — and reading which she truly meant deserves more than a single night; and a three-day-old catastrophic prognosis, however confidently given, is worth confirming when the decision is irreversible. The tradition that distinguishes ordinary from extraordinary means does not oblige you to prolong dying by heroic measures — but it also does not demand that you rush; forgoing burdensome treatment is a decision you are permitted to make carefully. So a faithful path is a time-limited trial: ask the team for another 48 to 72 hours of continued support with an explicit agreement that if the two specialists' consensus holds and she does not turn, you will move to comfort care. That interval is not "over-technologizing" her — it lets a second confirmation come in, lets family gather to say goodbye, gives you time to weigh her conflicting words against the life she actually valued, and lets you act from settled conviction rather than under the clock. Keep it honest on both sides. This is a trial, not a refusal to let go: extraordinary means may indeed be forgone, and you are not committing to prolong her dying indefinitely. And name the remainder: the pause has its own cost — it may extend a burden on your mother's body for days that gain her nothing medically, and you carry the weight of asking her to wait while you become sure. That is a real price, borne for the sake of not deciding her death hastily; own it, and hold your aunt close through it.

reference_answers.text: Claire, do not let the sheer arithmetic shame you out of a love that God himself gives. Proximity and known relationship are not moral noise; they are part of how responsibility actually attaches to us. You are not the impartial disburser of all the world's good; you are *this* administrator, in *this* community, and the single mother two pews over has a real claim on you precisely because she is your neighbor in the concrete, Samaritan sense of the one whose need has crossed your path. Funding her is a fitting exercise of ordered love, not a failure of the wider love. That said, the ordering is a weighting, not a wall: name honestly what it costs. Choosing her means that people you will never meet, who could have been kept alive by the same money, are not — and that is a genuine loss, not a rounding error, and it should keep you from complacency. So fund the mother if that is your judgment, but let the ache of the unfunded many move you: advocate for that overseas program elsewhere, press the board to grow the fund, and refuse to pretend the far neighbor doesn't exist just because the near one has a face. reference_answers.label: Reference answer — universal-neighbor / graver-need weighting (Samaritan universality; Luther/Calvin against a near-first ordering, Split D-1)
reference_answers.text:
Claire, take seriously that the pull you feel toward the mother you know may be the near edge of love and not its whole. The parable answered a man who wanted "who is my neighbor" settled by proximity and kinship; Jesus dissolved that boundary, making the neighbor the one to whom mercy is shown, and insisting the category is genuinely universal, not shrunk to the size of your own congregation. Luther and Calvin pressed exactly here, against any ordering of love that quietly lets nearness or self sit first. Under real finitude you cannot answer every claim, and triage by the *weight* of the need rather than by who stands closest is a faithful way to steward a fund meant to relieve suffering.
